key_terms.meaning: SI: a spark lights a premixed charge. CI: fuel sprayed into air hot from compression ignites by itself.
V<sub>s</sub> = (π/4)d²L; displacement = V<sub>s</sub> × number of cylinders
S̄<sub>p</sub> = 2LN (L in m, N in rev/s)
mep = W<sub>net</sub>/V<sub>s</sub>; indicated power = mep × V<sub>s</sub> × cycles per second
N/2 for a four-stroke, N for a two-stroke (N in rev/s)
sweeping burnt gas out of a two-stroke cylinder with fresh charge or air
SI: throttle sets the mixture quantity. CI: fuel quantity sets the mixture strength
inlet = lead + 180° + lag; exhaust = lead + 180° + lag; overlap = inlet lead + exhaust lag
exhaust and transfer symmetric about BDC; piston-controlled inlet symmetric about TDC
ideal processes with the real mixture: variable specific heats, dissociation, change of moles
η<sub>i</sub> = W<sub>i</sub>/Q<sub>f</sub>; η<sub>m</sub> = W<sub>b</sub>/W<sub>i</sub>; η<sub>b</sub> = η<sub>i</sub>η<sub>m</sub>

takeaways: An IC engine is classified on several independent bases (ignition, strokes, cycle, fuel, cooling, air supply, cylinders); an engine takes one label from each.

Bore, stroke, clearance volume and compression ratio describe the cylinder: V<sub>s</sub> = (π/4)d²L and r = (V<sub>s</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>)/V<sub>c</sub>; mep turns work per cycle into a size-free pressure.
A four-stroke fires once in two revolutions, a two-stroke once per revolution; the two-stroke’s extra power is cut by ports and short-circuiting, and two-stroke diesels scavenge with blown air.
SI engines compress a premixed charge (r 8 to 12, knock-limited, throttled); CI engines compress air alone (r 16 to 22) and ignite injected fuel by the heat of compression.
Valves open early and close late to use gas inertia: open periods are lead + 180° + lag, and the overlap near TDC is small in throttled SI idle and naturally aspirated diesels, larger with boost.
Piston-controlled ports are symmetric about their dead centre; the exhaust opens first and closes last.
Firing interval is 720°/n; an inline four can fire only 1-3-4-2 or 1-2-4-3, and the camshaft turns at half crank speed.
At equal r, Otto > dual > Diesel; at equal peak pressure, Diesel > dual > Otto, which is the fair comparison for real engines.

Variable specific heats and dissociation lower the fuel-air cycle below the air-standard value; time, heat, blowdown and pumping losses lower the actual cycle further, and friction separates indicated from brake work.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for labelled sketches here: the cylinder with its parts, the two-stroke ports, the valve and port timing circles, the firing-order chart and the p-v and T-s diagrams of the cycles. Numerical questions are almost always Otto, Diesel or dual cycle problems worked to the efficiency and mean effective pressure.

bank.q: Classify IC engines on at least six bases, giving the types and one Indian example for each, and explain why the bases are independent of one another.
outline: Bases: ignition, strokes, cycle, fuel, cooling, air supply, cylinder arrangement (also fuel supply, valve location, speed, use)
Types with an example for each
One engine described under every basis
Independence: one label from each list
answer: An IC engine is classified by asking several separate questions about it. Each question gives one basis, and an engine takes one answer from each.

answer.text: The main bases, their types and examples:

head: Basis
Types
Example
rows: SI engines Otto; slow ship diesels Diesel; fast diesels dual
petrol; diesel; CNG or LPG; alcohol blends; bi-fuel
car inline four; large gensets V
side valve (L, T, F head); overhead valve (I head)

answer: SI engines burn a fuel that is easily vaporised and premixed (petrol, CNG); a spark fixes the moment of burning. CI engines compress air to about 16 to 22 times and spray diesel into it; the fuel self-ignites.
A four-stroke engine has a separate stroke for each job and fires once in two revolutions; a two-stroke does the gas exchange through ports near BDC and fires once every revolution.
Supercharged and turbocharged engines both force in denser air: a supercharger is driven from the crankshaft, a turbocharger by an exhaust turbine.

One engine on every basis, the scooter of the history chapter: SI, two-stroke, Otto cycle, petrol, air-cooled, naturally aspirated, single cylinder, carburetted, piston-ported. A highway truck engine: CI, four-stroke, dual cycle, diesel, liquid-cooled, turbocharged, inline six, direct injection, I head.

Independence: changing one answer does not force another. A two-stroke may be SI (scooter) or CI (ship engine); a CI engine may be air-cooled (small tractor engines) or water-cooled; a CNG engine is SI although it is used in buses that were once diesel. So an answer that lists one long tree mixing these bases is wrong in principle: each basis is its own list.
Check: the scooter takes exactly one label from each of the seven main lists (Figure 1.1.1), and none of its labels contradicts another.

bank.q: With a neat sketch, name the main components of an IC engine and state the function and the usual material of each, giving the reason for the material.
outline: Labelled sketch of one cylinder
Block, liner, head, gasket, piston, rings, gudgeon pin, connecting rod, crankshaft, bearings, flywheel, camshaft, valves, manifolds, sump
Function and material for each
Reason: weight, fatigue, heat, wear
answer: Sketch: draw one cylinder as in Figure 1.2.1, with the cylinder head carrying the inlet and exhaust valves and the spark plug (or injector), the block with its coolant jacket, the piston with rings and gudgeon pin at BDC, the connecting rod, the crank pin and crankshaft, and mark TDC, BDC, bore and stroke.

head: Part
Function
Material and reason
rows: holds cylinders, coolant passages and main bearings
grey cast iron: rigid, cheap, damps vibration; aluminium alloy where weight matters
renewable sliding surface for the piston
centrifugally cast alloy iron: wear-resistant, graphite helps sliding
closes the cylinder; carries valves, ports, plug or injector
cast iron or aluminium alloy (conducts heat away from the chamber)
seals gas, water and oil between head and block
multi-layer steel or copper with fibre
takes the gas force and passes it to the rod
aluminium-silicon alloy: light, conducts heat; low expansion from silicon
compression rings seal gas; oil ring scrapes oil
fine-grain cast iron or steel: springy when hot, slides well
case-hardened steel: hard surface, tough core
turns the piston push into a crank-pin force
forged steel: strong in fatigue under alternating load
forged alloy steel or SG iron; journals hardened and ground
support crank and rods on an oil film
steel shell lined with white metal or copper-lead: conformable, embeds dirt
cast iron or steel: mass at a large radius
time the opening of the gas passages
camshaft chilled cast iron or steel; exhaust valve chromium-silicon steel for heat
lead charge in and exhaust out
inlet aluminium or plastic; exhaust cast iron or steel
house the crank; hold the oil
cast iron, aluminium or pressed steel

answer: The piston reverses direction twice per revolution, so its inertia force rises with the square of speed; aluminium alloy, at about one third the density of cast iron, keeps this force small and carries heat from the crown to the rings quickly.
The crankshaft and connecting rod are loaded, unloaded and reloaded on every cycle, millions of times, so fatigue strength decides the material: forging lines the grain along the part and raises it.
The exhaust valve sits in gas at several hundred degrees Celsius and is cooled only through its seat and stem; chromium and silicon keep the steel strong and resist scaling at that temperature.

The block must hold the bore round and the bearings in line under the gas load; the stiffness and damping of cast iron do this cheaply, and an aluminium block needs iron liners where the piston slides.
Check: every part in the sketch appears in the table, and each material is justified by the one demand that dominates for that part: weight, fatigue, heat or wear.

bank.q: Explain with sketches the working of a two-stroke SI engine and a two-stroke CI engine, and compare two-stroke and four-stroke engines.
outline: Crankcase-scavenged SI engine: three ports, upward and downward strokes
Blowdown, scavenging and short-circuiting
CI two-stroke: blower, air scavenging, uniflow with exhaust valves
Comparison table
answer: Sketch the crankcase-scavenged engine as in Figure 1.3.1: cylinder with spark plug, exhaust port high on one side, transfer port a little lower on the other side joined by a passage to the sealed crankcase, and an inlet port into the crankcase.

Upward stroke (BDC to TDC): the piston covers the transfer port and then the exhaust port and compresses the charge trapped above it. Below the piston the crankcase volume grows, its pressure falls below atmospheric, and the piston skirt uncovers the inlet port near TDC, so fresh mixture enters the crankcase. The spark fires just before TDC.

Downward stroke (TDC to BDC): the burning gas drives the piston down, the power stroke, while the underside of the piston compresses the crankcase charge. About 60° before BDC the exhaust port opens and most burnt gas escapes (blowdown). About 45° before BDC the transfer port opens and the crankcase charge flows into the cylinder, pushing out the remaining burnt gas (scavenging). One cycle takes one revolution, 360°CA.

Because exhaust and transfer ports are open together, part of the fresh mixture leaves with the exhaust (short-circuiting). This wastes petrol and raises unburnt hydrocarbon emissions; deflector pistons and loop-scavenged ports reduce it.

Two-stroke CI engine: it scavenges with air, so short-circuiting wastes no fuel, and fuel is injected after the ports close. It cannot use crankcase compression because the crankcase holds the lubricating oil; a Roots blower or a turbocharger delivers air at above atmospheric pressure to an air box. Large engines use uniflow scavenging: air enters through ports round the bottom of the liner and leaves through exhaust valves in the head, sweeping the cylinder in one direction. Sketch it with inlet ports at the bottom, two exhaust valves at the top and the injector in the centre of the head.

head: Feature
Four-stroke
Two-stroke
rows: Power strokes per cylinder per revolution
ports; exhaust valves in uniflow diesels
Power for the same size and speed
oil in petrol, or separate oiler

answer: Numbers for the power claim: at 5000 rev/min two 150 cm³ cylinders with indicated mep 6 bar (four-stroke) and 4.5 bar (two-stroke) give 6 × 10⁵ × 150 × 10⁻⁶ × 5000/120 = 3.75 kW and 4.5 × 10⁵ × 150 × 10⁻⁶ × 5000/60 = 5.63 kW: 1.5 times, not twice.
Check: the two-stroke still has exactly two strokes per cycle; each stroke simply does two jobs, one above and one below the piston.

bank.q: Explain the working principle of SI and CI engines with p-V diagrams and compare the two engines on at least eight points.
outline: SI: premixed charge, throttle, spark, flame front
CI: air only, high r, injection, ignition delay
p-V sketches with the spark and injection points marked
Comparison table
answer: SI engine: the intake stroke draws in a petrol-air mixture whose quantity is set by the throttle. Compression to r = 8 to 12 raises its pressure and temperature but not enough for it to ignite by itself. The spark plug fires 10° to 40° before TDC, and a flame front spreads across the chamber in a few milliseconds; the pressure peaks just after TDC. Expansion gives the work, and the exhaust stroke clears the cylinder.

CI engine: the intake draws in air only, with no throttle. Compression to r = 16 to 22 heats it; ideal compression from 300 K gives 953 K at r = 18, well above the self-ignition temperature of diesel. Injection starts about 5° to 25° before TDC; after an ignition delay of about a millisecond the spray ignites at many points, and the rest burns as it mixes. Load is changed by changing the fuel quantity.

p-V sketches: for both, draw the intake line just below atmospheric, the compression curve, a steep rise near TDC and the expansion curve. Mark the spark point on the SI compression line and the start of injection on the CI line. The SI curve reaches about 18 bar by the end of compression at r = 8; the CI curve, from a much smaller clearance volume, reaches about 57 bar at r = 18 before combustion begins.

head: Point
SI engine
CI engine
rows: carburettor or injector before the cylinder

answer: Reasons behind the main differences: the premixed SI charge would knock if compressed further, so its r and hence its efficiency are lower; the CI engine needs its high r to light the fuel, which gives better efficiency but higher pressures, heavier parts and lower speed. The throttle costs the SI engine pumping work at part load, which is why it is thirsty in slow traffic.

Check with numbers: T₂ = 300 × 9<sup>0.4</sup> = 722 K at r = 9 and 300 × 18<sup>0.4</sup> = 953 K at r = 18; the higher temperature and 2.6 times the pressure make the diesel ignition delay short enough to be useful.

bank.q: Draw and explain the valve timing diagrams of a four-stroke SI engine and a four-stroke CI engine, marking lead, lag and overlap, and give the reasons for each event.
outline: Circle diagram, TDC at top, crank clockwise
IVO before TDC, IVC after BDC, EVO before BDC, EVC after TDC
Spark and injection marked
Reasons: inertia, ram effect, blowdown, scavenging of clearance
SI and CI angles compared; overlap at idle and with boost
answer: Draw a circle with TDC at the top and BDC at the bottom, the crank turning clockwise; mark the inlet arc at a smaller radius and the exhaust arc at a larger one so the overlap near TDC shows clearly (Figure 1.5.1, left).

answer.text: Typical angles used for the two diagrams:

answer: Inlet opens before TDC (lead): the valve needs time to lift, so starting early gives a full opening when the piston moves down and the cylinder pressure falls.

Inlet closes after BDC (lag): the column of charge in the inlet pipe is moving fast and keeps flowing in by its inertia, the ram effect, for some degrees after the piston has started up; closing late traps more charge and raises volumetric efficiency at speed.

Exhaust opens before BDC (lead): the burnt gas is still at 3 to 5 bar; letting it blow down before BDC means the piston pushes against low pressure on the exhaust stroke. The small loss of expansion work is less than the pumping work saved.
Exhaust closes after TDC (lag): the outgoing gas has momentum and keeps drawing burnt gas from the clearance space; with the inlet already open, this overlap helps start the new charge moving.

SI and CI differ in the reasons and sizes rather than the events. At idle a throttled SI engine has a low inlet pressure, so a long overlap lets exhaust flow back into the inlet; SI engines with tuned high-speed cams use more overlap and later inlet closing to breathe at speed. A naturally aspirated CI engine has very little piston-to-valve clearance at TDC because of its high r, and no boost to push air through, so its overlap is small; turbocharged diesels use a larger overlap to scavenge and cool with clean air. On the CI diagram the injection period replaces the spark.
Overlap trade-off: more overlap improves breathing at high speed but at low speed causes backflow and charge loss; this is why modern engines vary the cam timing with speed.
Check: the periods add up (inlet 230° and exhaust 235° for the SI engine), and the overlap is counted once, inside both periods.

bank.q: An engine works on the Otto cycle with a compression ratio of 9. At the start of compression the air is at 1 bar and 310 K, and the maximum temperature of the cycle is 2000 K. Taking γ = 1.4, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K and R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K, find the pressure and temperature at each point, the heat supplied, the net work, the thermal efficiency and the mean effective pressure.
outline: T₂ = T₁r<sup>γ−1</sup>, p₂ = p₁r<sup>γ</sup>
p₃ = p₂T₃/T₂
T₄ = T₃/r<sup>γ−1</sup>, p₄ = p₃/r<sup>γ</sup>
q<sub>in</sub>, q<sub>out</sub>, w, η
v₁ = RT₁/p₁, mep = w/(v₁ − v₂)
answer: Sketch first: a p-v diagram with 1→2 an isentrope rising to the left, 2→3 vertical at v₂, 3→4 an isentrope falling to the right, 4→1 vertical at v₁; and a T-s diagram where 1→2 and 3→4 are vertical and 2→3 and 4→1 are constant-volume curves. Mark the four states on both.

Given: r = 9, p₁ = 100 kPa, T₁ = 310 K, T₃ = 2000 K, γ = 1.4. Powers needed: 9<sup>0.4</sup> = 2.4082 and 9<sup>1.4</sup> = 21.674. Work per kg of air throughout, so heats are in kJ/kg and volumes in m³/kg.
Process 1→2, isentropic compression: T₂ = 310 × 2.4082 = 746.5 K; p₂ = 100 × 21.674 = 2167.4 kPa = 21.67 bar.
Process 2→3, constant-volume heat addition: p₃ = p₂ × T₃/T₂ = 2167.4 × 2000/746.5 = 5806.5 kPa = 58.07 bar.
Process 3→4, isentropic expansion: T₄ = 2000/2.4082 = 830.5 K; p₄ = 5806.5/21.674 = 267.9 kPa = 2.68 bar. (Check: p₄/p₁ = T₄/T₁ = 830.5/310 = 2.679.)
Heat supplied: q<sub>in</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₃ − T₂) = 0.718 × (2000 − 746.5) = 0.718 × 1253.5 = 900.0 kJ/kg.
Volumes: v₁ = RT₁/p₁ = 0.287 × 310/100 = 0.8897 m³/kg; v₂ = v₁/9 = 0.09886 m³/kg; swept volume v₁ − v₂ = 0.7908 m³/kg.
Mean effective pressure: mep = 526.3/0.7908 = 665.5 kPa = 6.65 bar.

Meaning of the result: only 58.5 per cent of the heat can become work even in this ideal cycle; the remaining 373.7 kJ/kg must be rejected because the gas leaves at 830.5 K, far above the 310 K it started from. Raising the maximum temperature would raise the work and the mep but not the efficiency, which depends on r alone.
Check: the energy balance closes (900.0 − 373.7 = 526.3 kJ/kg) and the two efficiency routes agree to four figures.

bank.q: An air-standard Diesel cycle has a compression ratio of 18, and the heat addition is cut off at 6 per cent of the stroke. At the start of compression the air is at 1 bar and 300 K. Find the cut-off ratio, the temperatures at the corners, the heat supplied, the efficiency and the mean effective pressure (γ = 1.4, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K). Compare the efficiency with an Otto cycle of the same r.
outline: ρ = 1 + k(r − 1) with k = 0.06
T₂, p₂, T₃ = ρT₂, T₄ = T₃(ρ/r)<sup>γ−1</sup>
q<sub>in</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>(T₃ − T₂), q<sub>out</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₄ − T₁)
η by heats and by formula
mep; Otto 68.5 % at r = 18
answer: Sketch: on p-v, 1→2 an isentrope, 2→3 a horizontal line at 57.2 bar from v₂ to v₃, 3→4 an isentrope to v₁, 4→1 vertical. On T-s, 2→3 is a constant-pressure curve, flatter than a constant-volume curve through the same point.
Cut-off ratio: take v₂ = 1 unit, so v₁ = 18 and the stroke is 17 units. Cut-off at 6 per cent of the stroke gives v₃ = 1 + 0.06 × 17 = 2.02, so ρ = v₃/v₂ = 2.02.
Process 2→3 at constant pressure: T₃ = ρT₂ = 2.02 × 953.3 = 1925.7 K.
Process 3→4, isentropic to v₁: T₄ = T₃(v₃/v₁)<sup>0.4</sup> = T₃(ρ/r)<sup>0.4</sup> = 1925.7 × (2.02/18)<sup>0.4</sup> = 1925.7 × 0.41690 = 802.8 K.

Comparison: an Otto cycle with r = 18 would give 1 − 0.3147 = 68.5 %. The Diesel cycle is 5.4 points lower at the same r because the bracket 1.1737 multiplies the heat rejected; adding heat while the piston moves out leaves less expansion for that heat.

Effect of cut-off: if the cut-off were later (more fuel), ρ and the bracket would grow and the efficiency would fall further; so in the ideal cycle a diesel’s efficiency rises as its load falls, the opposite of a throttled petrol engine.
Check: p₄ = p₁T₄/T₁ = 802.8/300 = 2.68 bar, and the energy balance closes to 0.1 kJ/kg.

bank.q: A dual combustion cycle has a compression ratio of 14, a pressure ratio α = 1.5 in the constant-volume part of heat addition and a cut-off ratio ρ = 1.6. It starts at 1 bar and 300 K. Find the temperatures at all points, the heat supplied in each part, the efficiency and the mean effective pressure (γ = 1.4, c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K).
outline: Points 1 to 5: 1→2 isentropic, 2→3 constant v, 3→4 constant p, 4→5 isentropic, 5→1 constant v
T₃ = αT₂, T₄ = ρT₃, T₅ = T₄(ρ/r)<sup>γ−1</sup>
q at constant v and constant p
η by heats and by formula
mep
answer: Sketch: on p-v the cycle has five corners: an isentrope 1→2, a vertical rise 2→3, a horizontal line 3→4 at the peak pressure, an isentrope 4→5 and a vertical drop 5→1. On T-s the heat addition is a steep constant-volume curve followed by a flatter constant-pressure curve.
Numbering: 1→2 isentropic compression, 2→3 heat at constant volume (α = p₃/p₂), 3→4 heat at constant pressure (ρ = v₄/v₃), 4→5 isentropic expansion to v₁, 5→1 heat rejected at constant volume.
Point 3: p₃ = 1.5 × 40.23 = 60.35 bar (the peak pressure); T₃ = αT₂ = 1.5 × 862.1 = 1293.2 K.

Heat at constant volume: 0.718 × (1293.2 − 862.1) = 0.718 × 431.1 = 309.5 kJ/kg. Heat at constant pressure: 1.005 × (2069.1 − 1293.2) = 1.005 × 775.9 = 779.8 kJ/kg. Total q<sub>in</sub> = 1089.3 kJ/kg.

Share of heat: 309.5 of 1089.3 kJ/kg (28 per cent) is added at constant volume and 72 per cent at constant pressure, a typical split for a fast diesel whose first burst of burning is nearly at constant volume.

Check: the Otto cycle at r = 14 would give 1 − 1/2.8738 = 65.2 %; the dual cycle at 62.5 % lies below it, as it must at equal r, and above a Diesel cycle that put all 1089 kJ/kg in at constant pressure.

bank.q: In a two-stroke petrol engine running at 4000 rev/min, the exhaust port opens 62° before BDC, the transfer port opens 50° before BDC and the piston-controlled inlet port opens 50° before TDC. Draw the port timing diagram and find the open period of each port, the blowdown angle, the angle for which the exhaust is open after the transfer port closes, and the time for each.
outline: Symmetry about BDC (exhaust, transfer) and TDC (inlet)
Blowdown 12°, post-transfer 12°
Time per degree at 4000 rev/min
answer: Draw a circle with TDC at the top and BDC at the bottom, crank clockwise. Piston-controlled ports open and close at equal angles on either side of the dead centre that uncovers them, so the exhaust and transfer arcs are symmetric about BDC and the inlet arc about TDC (Figure 1.5.1, right, has the same form).
Exhaust port: opens 62° before BDC, closes 62° after BDC; open period = 62 + 62 = 124°CA.
Transfer port: opens 50° before BDC, closes 50° after BDC; open period = 100°CA.
Inlet port: opens 50° before TDC, closes 50° after TDC; open period = 100°CA.

Blowdown, from exhaust opening to transfer opening: 62 − 50 = 12°CA. During it the cylinder pressure falls below the crankcase pressure, so the charge does not blow back into the crankcase when the transfer port opens.

Exhaust open after the transfer closes: from 50° to 62° after BDC = 12°CA, the same as the blowdown because of the symmetry. In this period fresh charge can leave through the exhaust with nothing entering behind it.
Time per degree: at 4000 rev/min the crank turns 4000/60 × 360 = 24 000° per second, so 1° takes 1/24 000 s = 0.0417 ms.

Sequence on the diagram, going clockwise from TDC: inlet closes (50° after TDC), exhaust opens (118° after TDC), transfer opens (130°), BDC (180°), transfer closes (230°), exhaust closes (242°), inlet opens (310°).

Why the ports are placed this way: the exhaust port is higher in the wall than the transfer port, so the piston uncovers it first on the way down and covers it last on the way up. That order gives the blowdown before transfer, but it also forces the post-transfer exhaust period, because a piston edge cannot close the higher port first. Reed valves, rotary valves or an exhaust power valve are used when unsymmetric timing is wanted.

Comment: the whole scavenging process, transfer port open, lasts only about 4 ms at this speed, which is why the port shapes and the crankcase pressure matter so much in a two-stroke, and why some charge is always lost through the exhaust.
Check: each symmetric period is twice its lead angle, and the event angles listed above increase steadily round the circle with no overlap of the inlet with the transfer.

bank.q: For an inline four-cylinder four-stroke engine, show why the firing orders 1-3-4-2 and 1-2-4-3 are possible and 1-2-3-4 is not. Prepare the stroke chart for 1-3-4-2 and find the time between firings at 3000 rev/min. What is the firing interval and a usual firing order of an inline six?
outline: Flat crank: 1 and 4 up, 2 and 3 down
Firing interval 180°
Next firing must come from the pair at TDC on compression
Stroke chart
answer: Firing interval: θ<sub>f</sub> = 720°/4 = 180°. The crankshaft of an inline four is flat: throws 1 and 4 point one way and throws 2 and 3 the opposite way (Figure 1.6.1). So pistons 1 and 4 reach TDC together, and 180° later pistons 2 and 3 do. Of each pair at TDC, one is ending compression and fires; the other is ending exhaust.

Let cylinder 1 fire at 0°. At 180° pistons 2 and 3 are at TDC, so either may fire next. At 360° pistons 1 and 4 are at TDC again; cylinder 1 has just finished its power stroke and exhaust, so cylinder 4 must fire. At 540° the other member of the 2-3 pair fires.

So the orders are 1-3-4-2 (3 fires at 180°) or 1-2-4-3 (2 fires at 180°). In 1-2-3-4 the third firing, at 360°, would have to be cylinder 3, but at 360° only pistons 1 and 4 are at TDC; so this order cannot be made with this crankshaft.

answer.text: Stroke chart for 1-3-4-2 (P power, E exhaust, I intake, C compression):

answer: Each column has exactly one P, so one power stroke arrives every 180°; each row runs P, E, I, C in order, so each cylinder completes one cycle in 720°.
Time between firings at 3000 rev/min: 3000/60 = 50 rev/s, so half a revolution takes 0.5/50 = 0.010 s = 10 ms.

Why 1-3-4-2 is preferred: consecutive firings are never in neighbouring cylinders at one end (1 then 3, 3 then 4, 4 then 2), so the main bearing between two cylinders is not loaded by two power strokes in a row, the twisting of the shaft is spread, and the exhaust pulses are spaced in the manifold.

Inline six: θ<sub>f</sub> = 720°/6 = 120°; throws are in pairs 1-6, 2-5 and 3-4 at 120° to each other; the usual order is 1-5-3-6-2-4, which alternates between the front three and the rear three cylinders. At 3000 rev/min the firings are (1/3)/50 = 6.67 ms apart.
Check: the chart agrees with the worked example of the firing order chapter, where in the first half-turn cylinder 1 is on power, 3 on compression, 4 on intake and 2 on exhaust.

bank.q: An Otto cycle with r = 8 starts at 1 bar and 300 K and receives 1500 kJ/kg of heat at constant volume. Find the peak temperature and pressure (a) with constant c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K and (b) with c<sub>v</sub> = 0.71 + 0.0002 T kJ/kg·K. Explain how variable specific heats and dissociation make the fuel-air cycle efficiency lower than the air-standard value.
outline: Constant c<sub>v</sub>: T₃ = T₂ + q/c<sub>v</sub>
Variable c<sub>v</sub>: integrate and solve the quadratic
Peak T and p lower
Effects on work and efficiency; dissociation; mixture strength
answer: Compression (taken as isentropic with γ = 1.4 in both cases): T₂ = 300 × 8<sup>0.4</sup> = 300 × 2.2974 = 689.2 K; p₂ = 1 × 8<sup>1.4</sup> = 18.38 bar.

answer.text: (b) Variable c<sub>v</sub>: the heat is the integral of c<sub>v</sub> dT.

answer: Peak pressure (b): p₃ = 18.38 × 2192/689.2 = 58.5 bar.

Why efficiency falls: with variable specific heat the same heat gives a peak 586 K cooler and 15.6 bar lower, so the gas starts its expansion from a lower pressure. γ also falls at high temperature, so the expansion line is flatter and the gas leaves the cylinder hotter; more of the heat is rejected and less becomes work.

Dissociation: above about 1600 K, CO₂ and H₂O split into CO, H₂, O₂ and OH, absorbing heat at the peak. Some of it is released again as the gas cools, but late in the stroke where it does little work. It is strongest near the chemically correct mixture.

Mixture strength: lean mixtures burn cooler, with less specific-heat rise and dissociation, so efficiency rises as the mixture is leaned; maximum power comes slightly rich, about φ = 1.1 to 1.2, where all the air is used.

Result: for a chemically correct petrol mixture the fuel-air cycle efficiency is typically about four fifths of the air-standard value at the same r, and the effect of r on it has the same trend as in the air-standard cycle.
Check: both cases start from the same T₂ = 689.2 K and receive the same 1500 kJ/kg; only the property of the gas differs, so the whole difference is due to c<sub>v</sub>.

bank.q: Compare the Otto, Diesel and dual cycles on p-v and T-s diagrams (a) for the same compression ratio and heat input and (b) for the same maximum pressure and heat input, and judge which comparison is fair for real engines.
outline: Common point 1 and common heat-rejection line on T-s
η = 1 − q<sub>out</sub>/q<sub>in</sub>
(a) Otto > dual > Diesel
(b) Diesel > dual > Otto
Numbers from the worked examples
Peak pressure limits real engines
answer: Method: draw all three cycles from the same state 1. They all reject heat along the same constant-volume line through state 1, so on a T-s diagram the heat rejected is the area under that line between state 1 and the end of expansion. With the same heat input, η = 1 − q<sub>out</sub>/q<sub>in</sub> is highest for the cycle whose expansion ends farthest to the left, rejecting least heat.

(a) Same compression ratio and heat input. On p-v all three compress along the same line 1→2. Otto adds all its heat at v₂, the smallest volume; Diesel adds it at constant pressure while the volume grows; dual is in between. On T-s, the constant-volume line through 2 is steeper than the constant-pressure line, so for equal areas under the heat-addition lines the Otto cycle ends heat addition at the smallest entropy, and its expansion ends lowest on the rejection line. Result: q<sub>out</sub> is smallest for Otto, so η<sub>Otto</sub> > η<sub>dual</sub> > η<sub>Diesel</sub>.
Numbers: at r = 16, η<sub>Otto</sub> = 1 − 1/16<sup>0.4</sup> = 67.0 %, and the Diesel cycle with ρ = 2 gives 61.4 %.

(b) Same maximum pressure and heat input. Now the Diesel cycle can use a much higher compression ratio before reaching the pressure limit, so its compression line goes higher. On T-s all three meet the same peak-pressure line; the Diesel cycle reaches it by compression and adds heat along it, the Otto cycle reaches it by constant-volume heating from a lower compression. The Diesel cycle then rejects the least heat: η<sub>Diesel</sub> > η<sub>dual</sub> > η<sub>Otto</sub>. The same order holds for the same maximum pressure and maximum temperature.

answer.text: Numbers from the two worked examples of the air-standard chapter (both from 1 bar and 300 K):

answer: With nearly the same peak pressure (48.0 and 48.5 bar) the Diesel cycle is 4.9 points more efficient and gives 25 per cent more work per kg (Figure 1.7.1), although at equal r it would be 5.6 points worse.

Judgement: comparison (a) is easy but unfair to real engines, because no real CI engine runs at an SI compression ratio, and SI engines cannot raise r without knock. What limits a real engine is the peak pressure its block, head, rod and bearings can carry, and the peak temperature its materials can stand. So comparison (b), at the same maximum pressure (and temperature), is the fair one, and it correctly predicts that CI engines are more efficient.
The dual cycle is the best model of a real high-speed diesel, which burns part of its fuel rapidly near TDC (nearly constant volume) and the rest as it is injected (nearly constant pressure).
Check: the two numerical cases reproduce both orders: Otto wins at equal r (67.0 against 61.4 %), Diesel wins at equal peak pressure (61.4 against 56.5 %).

bank.q: Compare the air-standard cycle, the fuel-air cycle and the actual cycle of an SI engine. Explain each loss that separates them with an indicator diagram, and evaluate their size with numbers.
outline: Assumptions removed at each step
Fuel-air: variable specific heats, dissociation, moles, mixture
Actual: time loss, heat loss, blowdown, pumping, incomplete combustion, leakage, friction
Indicator diagram sketch
Efficiency ladder with numbers
answer: Air-standard cycle: a fixed mass of air, an ideal gas with constant specific heats, heat added instantaneously at constant volume, isentropic compression and expansion, no gas exchange. At r = 8 it gives 1 − 1/8<sup>0.4</sup> = 56.5 %, the ceiling for an engine with this compression ratio.

Fuel-air cycle: the same ideal processes but with the real working fluid. (1) Specific heats rise with temperature, so the same heat gives a lower peak; with c<sub>v</sub> = 0.71 + 0.00019 T the air-standard example’s heat of 797.5 kJ/kg reaches 1553 K and 41.4 bar instead of 1800 K and 48.0 bar. (2) Dissociation absorbs heat at the peak. (3) The number of moles changes on burning, slightly raising the pressure. (4) Residual gas and the mixture strength set the actual charge. Typical result: about four fifths of the air-standard value, so roughly 45 % at r = 8.
Actual cycle (sketch the indicator diagram over the ideal one, as in Figure 1.8.1): the solid loop lies inside the dashed ideal loop. The losses, each visible as an area:

head: Loss
Cause
Where on the diagram
rows: burning takes 40° to 60°; spark must be advanced
heat to cylinder walls, head and piston
corner cut off at the end of expansion
intake below and exhaust above atmospheric
small negative loop at the bottom
unburnt fuel, gas past the rings
not on the diagram: indicated minus brake

answer: Numbers from the fuel-air chapter’s second worked example (500 cm³, 3000 rev/min): main loop 380 J, pumping loop 18 J, net indicated W<sub>i</sub> = 362 J; fuel energy 0.0255 g × 44 MJ/kg = 1122 J; brake work 290 J.

Evaluation: the largest single gap between fuel-air and actual is usually the heat loss, followed by the time loss and, at part throttle, the pumping loss. The fuel-air step is set by the gas itself and cannot be removed by better hardware; the actual-cycle losses are what engine designers fight with faster burning, better sealing, lower friction and less throttling.
Friction power in the example: (362 − 290) × 3000/120 = 1800 W, out of 9.05 kW indicated.
Check: brake efficiency η<sub>i</sub> × η<sub>m</sub> = 0.323 × 0.801 = 0.258 agrees with 290/1122, and the losses fall in the order air-standard > fuel-air > indicated > brake.

bank.q: Explain why a CI engine needs a much higher compression ratio than an SI engine, and evaluate the effect of raising the compression ratio on efficiency, knock, peak pressure and the engine structure, using numbers.
outline: Self-ignition needs hot, dense air at the end of compression
T₂ and p₂ at r = 8, 10, 16, 20
Ignition delay falls steeply with T and p
Otto efficiency gain with diminishing returns
SI knock limit; CI pressure and NOx limit; practical ranges
answer: A CI engine has no spark; the fuel must ignite by itself soon after injection. That needs air at the end of compression that is far hotter than the fuel’s self-ignition temperature (about 520 K in still air) and dense, so that the ignition delay is a fraction of a millisecond. Only a high compression ratio provides this, and the engine must also start from cold with heat lost to cold walls.

answer.text: Ideal end-of-compression states from 1 bar and 300 K, and ideal Otto efficiency:

answer: Ignition delay falls steeply with temperature and pressure. A standard correlation (Wolfer’s) gives about 7 ms at 722 K and 21.7 bar (r = 9) but about 0.5 ms at 953 K and 57 bar (r = 18). At 3000 rev/min 7 ms is about 130°CA, far too late to be useful; 0.5 ms is about 9°CA. So a diesel needs r of 16 to 22, the higher values for small, fast engines that lose more heat and must start cold.

An SI engine needs the opposite: its premixed charge must not ignite by itself. Raising r heats the end gas, and above about 10 to 12 (depending on octane, chamber shape and cooling) the end gas self-ignites before the flame reaches it, which is knock. So SI ratios stay at 8 to 12.

Effect on efficiency: the table shows the gain from r but with diminishing returns: 8 → 10 adds 3.7 points, 16 → 20 adds only 2.8 points for a larger step. In real engines the gain levels off further because friction and heat loss grow with peak pressure and surface-to-volume ratio.

Effect on peak pressure and structure: p₂ alone rises from 18 bar at r = 8 to 66 bar at r = 20, and combustion adds more; diesel peak pressures are far higher than petrol ones. Heavier blocks, heads, rods, crankshafts and bearings are needed, the moving masses limit the speed, and the engine costs more. Higher combustion temperatures also raise NOx.

Evaluation: for SI engines, r is set by knock, and higher-octane fuel (or direct injection, cooled charge and faster burning) lets it rise; for CI engines, r is set from below by reliable cold starting and from above by peak pressure, NOx and friction, which is why modern diesels have lowered r towards 15 to 17 with better injection and turbocharging.
Conclusion: the compression ratio is the main reason the CI engine is more efficient and heavier, and the SI engine lighter, faster and cheaper; neither can simply copy the other’s ratio.
Check: T₂ = 300 × 18<sup>0.4</sup> = 953 K and p₂ = 18<sup>1.4</sup> = 57.2 bar, as used for the delay estimate; the efficiency column follows 1 − r<sup>−0.4</sup>.

glossary.def: A heat engine that burns its fuel inside the working cylinder, so the hot products push the piston directly.
Ignition of a premixed fuel-air charge by an electric spark near the end of compression.
Self-ignition of fuel injected into air made hot by compression.
The inside diameter of the cylinder.
The distance the piston travels between TDC and BDC; twice the crank radius.
Top and bottom dead centre: the piston positions of smallest and largest cylinder volume.
The volume above the piston at TDC.
The volume the piston sweeps from TDC to BDC, (π/4)d²L.
Cylinder volume at BDC divided by that at TDC, (V<sub>s</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>)/V<sub>c</sub>.
The steady pressure that, acting on the piston over one stroke per cycle, would give the net work of the cycle.
Sweeping the burnt gas out of the cylinder with fresh charge or air, mainly in two-stroke engines.
Fresh charge flowing straight out of the exhaust port of a two-stroke during scavenging.
The two-stroke port through which charge passes from the crankcase into the cylinder.
Opening a valve before, and closing it after, the dead centre that bounds its stroke.
The crank angle near TDC when the inlet and exhaust valves are open together.
The rush of burnt gas out of the cylinder when the exhaust opens before BDC.
Charge that keeps flowing into the cylinder after BDC because of its inertia.
The sequence in which the cylinders of a multi-cylinder engine deliver their power strokes, such as 1-3-4-2.
The crank angle between two successive firings: 720°/n in a four-stroke engine.
A layout with both valves in the cylinder head above the piston.
An oil-filled tappet that takes up the valve clearance automatically.
An ideal cycle with air as an ideal gas of constant specific heats and heat added from outside instead of combustion.
The volume at the end of constant-pressure heat addition divided by that at its start.
α = p₃/p₂, the pressure rise of the constant-volume part of heat addition.
The breaking of CO₂ and H₂O into CO, H₂, O₂ and OH at high temperature, which absorbs heat.
The actual fuel-air ratio divided by the chemically correct one; above 1 is rich, below 1 lean.
The measured pressure against volume in a running cylinder; its net area is the indicated work.
The loss of work because burning takes a finite crank angle instead of happening at TDC.
Brake work divided by indicated work; it accounts for friction and auxiliaries.
